chapter_text:
CHAPTER 15 — CONSTITUTIONAL VALUES AND POLITICAL SYSTEM IN INDIA

Introduction

When India became independent on 15 August 1947, the framers had to decide what kind of country we would be. The CONSTITUTION OF INDIA, adopted on 26 November 1949 and brought into force on 26 January 1950, embodies that decision. It is the supreme law of the land — it defines the structure of government, the rights of citizens, the powers of states, and the values by which the nation will be governed. This chapter studies (i) the values that the Constitution embodies, (ii) the political system it sets up — a parliamentary, federal, democratic republic — and (iii) the meaning of citizenship in India.

15.1 THE INDIAN CONSTITUTION — A BRIEF BACKGROUND

The Constitution was drafted by a CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY of 299 elected representatives meeting between 1946 and 1949 under the chairmanship of Dr Rajendra Prasad. The DRAFTING COMMITTEE was chaired by Dr B.R. AMBEDKAR. The Assembly held 11 sessions over 2 years 11 months and 18 days, debating every clause. The Constitution finally adopted has 395 ARTICLES, 8 SCHEDULES and a PREAMBLE; today after many amendments it has 470+ articles and 12 schedules.

The Constitution drew inspiration from many sources — the Government of India Act 1935, the British parliamentary tradition, the US Bill of Rights, Irish Directive Principles, Canadian federalism, Australian concurrent list — yet it is distinctively Indian.

15.2 THE PREAMBLE — THE SOUL OF THE CONSTITUTION

The PREAMBLE is the short introductory statement that summarises the values of the Constitution. After the 42nd Amendment (1976) it reads:

  'WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens:
   JUSTICE, social, economic and political;
   LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;
   EQUALITY of status and of opportunity;
   and to promote among them all
   FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation;
   IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.'

Key VALUES in the Preamble:
 - SOVEREIGN — India is free to take its own decisions without outside interference.
 - SOCIALIST — committed to reducing inequalities and ensuring economic justice.
 - SECULAR — state has no official religion; all religions are equally respected.
 - DEMOCRATIC — government by the people, through elected representatives.
 - REPUBLIC — the head of state is elected, not hereditary.
 - JUSTICE — social, economic and political.
 - LIBERTY — of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
 - EQUALITY — of status and opportunity.
 - FRATERNITY — the spirit of brotherhood; dignity of the individual; unity and integrity of the nation.

15.3 THE INDIAN POLITICAL SYSTEM

India's political system has the following characteristic features:

(1) PARLIAMENTARY DEMOCRACY — modelled on the British (Westminster) system. The PRESIDENT is the constitutional (ceremonial) head of state. The PRIME MINISTER, leader of the majority party in Parliament, is the head of government. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the LOK SABHA (lower house).

(2) FEDERAL STRUCTURE — power is divided between the UNION (central) government and the STATES. The Constitution lists subjects in three lists (Seventh Schedule): UNION LIST (defence, foreign affairs, etc.), STATE LIST (police, public health, agriculture) and CONCURRENT LIST (education, marriage, forests — both can legislate). India is often described as 'quasi-federal' because it has strong unitary features (single citizenship, all-India services, emergency provisions).

(3) UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE — every citizen aged 18 or above (originally 21, reduced to 18 by the 61st Amendment in 1989) has the right to vote, regardless of caste, religion, sex or property.

(4) INDEPENDENT JUDICIARY — the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in each state. Judges enjoy security of tenure. They have the power of JUDICIAL REVIEW — to strike down laws that violate the Constitution.

(5) WRITTEN CONSTITUTION with FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS and DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES — rights of citizens are guaranteed; principles of governance are laid down.

(6) RULE OF LAW — all persons, including the highest officials, are equal before the law and subject to the same courts.

15.4 THREE ORGANS OF GOVERNMENT

The Constitution establishes three organs at both Union and State level, with separation of powers (though not as strict as in the US):

 - LEGISLATURE — makes laws. At the Union level: PARLIAMENT (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha + President). At State level: state legislature (Legislative Assembly + sometimes Legislative Council + Governor).
 - EXECUTIVE — implements laws. At the Union level: Prime Minister + Council of Ministers + President (constitutional head). At State level: Chief Minister + state Council of Ministers + Governor.
 - JUDICIARY — interprets laws and resolves disputes. SUPREME COURT (at top), HIGH COURTS in each state, SUBORDINATE COURTS at the district level.

15.5 CITIZENSHIP

The Constitution provides for SINGLE CITIZENSHIP — every person born in or naturalised in India is a CITIZEN OF INDIA, not separately a citizen of any state. This is unlike the United States, where one is a citizen of both the federation and one's state. Single citizenship strengthens national unity.

The Citizenship Act 1955 (with later amendments) specifies five ways to become a citizen: by BIRTH, by DESCENT, by REGISTRATION, by NATURALISATION, by INCORPORATION OF TERRITORY.

15.6 FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS, DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES AND DUTIES — A QUICK OVERVIEW

These are studied in detail in Chapter 16, but to introduce them here:

 - FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS (Part III, Articles 12-35) — six justiciable rights: right to equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.
 - DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY (Part IV, Articles 36-51) — non-justiciable but fundamental directions to government on how to make policy.
 - FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES (Part IVA, Article 51A) — ten (now eleven) duties of every citizen, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

SUMMARY

- The Indian Constitution, adopted 26 November 1949 and effective 26 January 1950, is the supreme law of the land.
- Drafted by the Constituent Assembly under Dr Rajendra Prasad; Drafting Committee headed by Dr B.R. Ambedkar.
- The Preamble declares India a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC committed to Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
- India's political system is parliamentary, federal, with universal adult franchise, independent judiciary, and rule of law.
- Three organs: Legislature (makes laws), Executive (implements), Judiciary (interprets).
- Single citizenship strengthens national unity.

chapter_summary.title: Constitutional Values and Political System in India — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Social Science (213) summary for Lesson 15 introduces the Constitution of India — its framing, the values declared in its Preamble, and the political system it establishes. India is a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic with a parliamentary form of government, a federal structure, an independent judiciary and a guarantee of fundamental rights.

sections.heading: Framing of the Constitution
bullets: The Constituent Assembly (299 members) met from December 1946 to November 1949 under the chairmanship of Dr Rajendra Prasad.
The Drafting Committee was headed by Dr B.R. AMBEDKAR — often called the 'Father of the Indian Constitution'.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 NOVEMBER 1949 (Constitution Day) and came into force on 26 JANUARY 1950 (Republic Day).
Originally 395 articles, 8 schedules; now after many amendments it has 470+ articles and 12 schedules.

sections.heading: The Preamble and constitutional values
bullets: Calls India a SOVEREIGN, SOCIALIST, SECULAR, DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC. ('Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.)

Promises JUSTICE (social, economic, political), LIBERTY (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), EQUALITY (of status and opportunity), and FRATERNITY (dignity of the individual and unity of the nation).
The Supreme Court has held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and reflects its basic structure.

sections.heading: Features of the Indian political system
bullets: PARLIAMENTARY DEMOCRACY — President is constitutional head; PM is head of government, responsible to Lok Sabha.
FEDERAL STRUCTURE — power divided between Union and States via three lists in the Seventh Schedule.
UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE — every citizen 18+ has the right to vote (lowered from 21 by the 61st Amendment, 1989).
INDEPENDENT JUDICIARY — Supreme Court, High Courts; judicial review.
RULE OF LAW — all are equal before the law; no one above it.

sections.heading: Three organs of government
bullets: LEGISLATURE — Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha + President) at Union; state legislatures at State.
EXECUTIVE — PM + Council of Ministers at Union; CM + state Council of Ministers at State.
JUDICIARY — Supreme Court at top; High Courts in each State; subordinate courts at district level.

sections.heading: Citizenship
bullets: India has SINGLE CITIZENSHIP — one is a citizen of India, not separately of any state. This strengthens national unity.
Five ways to acquire citizenship (Citizenship Act 1955): birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory.
Fundamental Rights are guaranteed to all citizens in Part III; some apply also to non-citizens.

key_takeaways: The Constitution of India, adopted 26 November 1949 and effective 26 January 1950, is the supreme law of the land.
It was drafted by the Constituent Assembly under Dr Rajendra Prasad; the Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar.
The Preamble declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic committed to Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
India has a parliamentary form of government with a federal structure, universal adult franchise, an independent judiciary and the rule of law.
Three organs — Legislature, Executive, Judiciary — operate at both Union and State levels.
India has single citizenship; citizenship can be acquired in five ways.

Free from external control — a sovereign state takes its own decisions in domestic and foreign affairs.
Committed to reducing inequalities of income, wealth and opportunity; ensuring economic justice for all citizens.
The state has no official religion and treats all religions equally; citizens have full freedom of religion.
Government by the people, directly or through elected representatives.
A state in which the head of state is elected, not hereditary.
A system of government in which the executive (PM and Cabinet) is drawn from and responsible to the elected legislature (Parliament).
A system in which political power is divided between a central (union) government and constituent (state) governments by a written constitution.
The right to vote granted to every adult citizen regardless of caste, religion, sex, education or property.
The power of courts to examine laws and government actions and to strike them down if they violate the Constitution.
The principle that all persons, including officials, are equal before the law and subject to the same courts.
Justiciable rights guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution — equality, freedom, against exploitation, religion, culture-and-education, constitutional remedies.
The Indian constitutional principle that a person is a citizen of India only, not separately of any state — unlike the US, which has dual citizenship.

questions.question: When was the Indian Constitution adopted and when did it come into force?
questions.answer: The Indian Constitution was ADOPTED by the Constituent Assembly on 26 NOVEMBER 1949 (now celebrated as Constitution Day or Samvidhan Divas) and came into FORCE on 26 JANUARY 1950 (Republic Day). The two-month gap was used to complete administrative arrangements and finalise certain provisions.

questions.question: Who was the chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Indian Constitution? Why is he honoured?
questions.answer: Dr B.R. AMBEDKAR was the chairman of the Drafting Committee. He is honoured as the 'FATHER (or Chief Architect) of the Indian Constitution' for his pivotal role in drafting it. His mastery of constitutional law, his deep understanding of social inequality, and his clarity of thought shaped almost every chapter. Born into the Dalit (untouchable) community, he overcame extraordinary obstacles to become a scholar, lawyer and statesman; his commitment to justice and equality is reflected throughout the Constitution.

questions.question: What does the Preamble declare about the nature of the Indian state?
questions.answer:
The Preamble declares India to be a 'SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC'. Each word carries weight:
 - SOVEREIGN — free from external control; takes its own decisions.
 - SOCIALIST — committed to economic justice and reducing inequalities.
 - SECULAR — no official religion; all religions equally respected.
 - DEMOCRATIC — government by the people through elected representatives.
 - REPUBLIC — head of state (President) is elected, not hereditary.
The words 'SOCIALIST' and 'SECULAR' were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

questions.question: What are the four ideals or 'values' that the Preamble promises to secure to all citizens?
questions.answer: (1) JUSTICE — social, economic and political. (2) LIBERTY — of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. (3) EQUALITY — of status and of opportunity. (4) FRATERNITY — assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation. These four ideals — Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity — are the philosophical pillars of the Indian Constitution. They echo (in a distinctively Indian setting) the values of the French Revolution.

questions.question: What is meant by 'parliamentary democracy'?
questions.answer: Parliamentary democracy is a system of government in which: (1) The EXECUTIVE (Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers) is drawn from and ACCOUNTABLE to the LEGISLATURE (Parliament). (2) The HEAD OF STATE (in India, the President) is a CONSTITUTIONAL head — performs ceremonial and limited functions, acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers. (3) The PM and Cabinet stay in office only as long as they enjoy the CONFIDENCE of the Lok Sabha — they can be removed by a vote of no confidence. (4) Elections are held at regular intervals to renew the people's mandate. India's parliamentary democracy is modelled on the British (Westminster) system, with adaptations.

questions.question: What is 'federalism'? How is it organised in India?
questions.answer:
Federalism is a system in which POLITICAL POWER is DIVIDED between a central (national / union) government and constituent (state) governments by a written constitution. Each level has its own sphere of authority.

In INDIA, the Seventh Schedule lists subjects in three categories:
 - UNION LIST — subjects on which only Parliament can legislate (e.g. defence, foreign affairs, currency, railways).
 - STATE LIST — subjects on which only state legislatures can legislate (e.g. police, public health, agriculture, land).
 - CONCURRENT LIST — subjects on which both Parliament and state legislatures can legislate (e.g. education, marriage, forests, criminal law). If a conflict arises, the Union law prevails.
India is called 'QUASI-FEDERAL' because it has strong unitary features: single citizenship, all-India services, emergency provisions that can centralise power, and the Union's overriding power on concurrent subjects.

questions.question: What is 'universal adult franchise'? At what age can Indians vote?
questions.answer: UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE is the right to vote granted to EVERY ADULT CITIZEN, regardless of caste, religion, sex, education, language, race or property. It is a foundational principle of democracy — every adult has an equal political voice. In India, the voting age was originally 21; the 61st CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT (1989) lowered it to 18 YEARS. So today, every Indian citizen aged 18 or above has the right to vote (subject to ordinary disqualifications like being declared mentally unsound, undischarged insolvent, or convicted of certain offences). India is the world's largest democracy by electorate.

questions.question: Name the three organs of government and state their primary functions.
questions.answer:
(1) LEGISLATURE — makes the laws. At the Union: PARLIAMENT (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha + President). At the State: state legislature (Legislative Assembly + sometimes Legislative Council + Governor).
(2) EXECUTIVE — implements the laws and runs day-to-day government. At Union: Prime Minister + Council of Ministers + President. At State: Chief Minister + state Council of Ministers + Governor. (The civil services, police etc. are part of the permanent executive.)
(3) JUDICIARY — interprets the laws and decides disputes. Supreme Court at top; High Court in each state; subordinate (district) courts below.

questions.question: What is 'single citizenship'? Why did the framers choose it?
questions.answer:
SINGLE CITIZENSHIP means that every Indian is a CITIZEN OF INDIA only — not separately of any state. So a person born in Kerala and living in Punjab is simply an Indian citizen, with the same rights and duties everywhere in the country. This is unlike the United States, where one is BOTH a citizen of the federation and a citizen of one's state — and state citizenship carries some distinct privileges.

The Indian framers chose single citizenship for several reasons: (1) to STRENGTHEN NATIONAL UNITY and discourage state chauvinism in a country with enormous diversity; (2) to ensure that every Indian has the same fundamental rights across the country; (3) to avoid the kind of state-based discrimination that plagued the US in the 19th century; (4) given the recent trauma of Partition, the priority was to forge ONE INDIAN PEOPLE.

questions.question: Explain the meaning and significance of 'secularism' as a value of the Indian Constitution.
questions.answer:
SECULARISM in the Indian Constitution means that the state has NO OFFICIAL RELIGION and treats all religions with EQUAL RESPECT. Citizens are free to profess, practise and propagate any religion of their choice.

KEY FEATURES of Indian secularism:
(1) NO STATE RELIGION — unlike Pakistan (Islamic Republic) or the UK (Anglican established church), India has no official religion.
(2) EQUAL RESPECT for ALL RELIGIONS (sarva dharma sambhava) — not hostility to religion but principled distance from all.
(3) FREEDOM of CONSCIENCE and worship for every citizen (Articles 25-28).
(4) Religious minorities have the right to establish and administer educational institutions (Article 30).
(5) The state can REGULATE secular activities associated with religious practice and intervene to reform social practices (e.g. banning untouchability, child marriage).

SIGNIFICANCE:
 - In a country with hundreds of religious communities (Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Jews and many tribal religions), secularism is essential to maintain social peace and ensure equal citizenship.
 - It guarantees that political power cannot be used to favour one religion over another.
 - After Partition, when the subcontinent was divided on religious lines, India's choice of secularism asserted that being Indian was independent of being Hindu/Muslim/Christian.
 - The word 'secular' was added explicitly to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, though the Constitution had always been secular in spirit.
The Supreme Court has held that secularism is part of the BASIC STRUCTURE of the Constitution — it cannot be amended away.

questions.question: State two key facts about the Constituent Assembly.
questions.answer: (1) It had 299 elected members, meeting from December 1946 to November 1949. (2) Dr Rajendra Prasad was its chairman; Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee. (3) It debated the Constitution for 2 years 11 months and 18 days. (4) It also acted as the Provisional Parliament of India until the first general elections in 1951-52.

questions.question: Explain what 'Democratic Republic' means in the Indian context.
questions.answer: DEMOCRATIC means government by the people: citizens choose their representatives through free and fair elections held at regular intervals, on the basis of universal adult franchise. The government is accountable to the people. REPUBLIC means the head of state — the President of India — is ELECTED, not hereditary. Together, 'Democratic Republic' contrasts India with both authoritarian regimes (where people do not choose their rulers) and monarchies (where the head of state inherits the position). The combination means: power flows from the people, and even the highest constitutional office is filled by election.

questions.question: What is meant by 'rule of law'? Why is it important?
questions.answer: RULE OF LAW means: (1) all persons — including the highest officials, the President, the Prime Minister, ministers, judges — are EQUAL BEFORE THE LAW; (2) no one is above the law; (3) laws are applied to all impartially and predictably; (4) no person can be punished except for a violation of a defined law, by a regular court, with due process. It is important because: it protects citizens from arbitrary action by powerful officials; it ensures predictability and fairness; it underpins democracy (rulers are subject to law, not above it); and it provides remedies — if the government acts unlawfully, citizens can take it to court.

questions.question: Distinguish the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary by their functions.
questions.answer:
LEGISLATURE MAKES LAW. At Union level, Parliament debates and passes laws (Acts). At state level, state legislatures pass state laws. The legislature also approves the budget and holds the executive accountable through questions and motions.

EXECUTIVE IMPLEMENTS LAW. The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers (at the Union) and the Chief Minister and state Council of Ministers (at the State) frame policy and direct the civil service to put laws into action. The executive also issues orders and rules within the framework of statutes.

JUDICIARY INTERPRETS LAW. Courts — the Supreme Court, High Courts and lower courts — resolve disputes, punish offences, and check whether laws and executive actions comply with the Constitution. Through JUDICIAL REVIEW, courts can strike down unconstitutional laws or actions.

questions.question: State the five ways to acquire Indian citizenship.
questions.answer: Under the Citizenship Act 1955: (1) BIRTH — by being born in India (subject to certain conditions about parentage post-2004). (2) DESCENT — born outside India to Indian-citizen parent(s). (3) REGISTRATION — for certain categories (e.g. persons of Indian origin living abroad, spouses of Indian citizens after 7 years' residence). (4) NATURALISATION — for foreigners who have lived in India for the qualifying period (currently 12 years) and meet other requirements. (5) INCORPORATION OF TERRITORY — when new territory is incorporated into India (e.g. Sikkim joined India in 1975), residents become Indian citizens.

questions.question: Briefly describe Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.
questions.answer:
FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS (Part III, Articles 12-35) — six justiciable rights guaranteed to every citizen: equality, freedom (speech, assembly etc.), against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies. 'Justiciable' means you can go to court if these are violated.

DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY (Part IV, Articles 36-51) — non-justiciable but fundamental DIRECTIONS to government on how to make policy. Include promoting welfare, securing the right to work and education, organising village panchayats, separating judiciary from executive, providing free legal aid, etc.

FUNDAMENTAL DUTIES (Part IVA, Article 51A) — ten (later eleven) duties of every citizen — to abide by the Constitution, cherish noble ideals of the freedom struggle, uphold sovereignty and integrity, render national service when called, promote harmony, protect environment, develop scientific temper, safeguard public property, etc. Added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

questions.question: Why is India called 'quasi-federal' rather than fully federal?
questions.answer:
India has FEDERAL features (two-tier government, written Constitution, division of powers in three lists, independent judiciary to settle disputes) but also strong UNITARY features that tilt the balance towards the Centre:
(1) SINGLE CITIZENSHIP — unlike the US.
(2) ALL-INDIA SERVICES (IAS, IPS, IFoS) — officers serve both Union and States but are controlled by the Union.
(3) EMERGENCY PROVISIONS — during national emergency (Article 352), the Centre can take over many state functions; President's rule (Article 356) can dismiss state governments.
(4) RESIDUARY POWERS rest with the Union, not the States.
(5) The CONCURRENT LIST — where conflict arises, UNION LAW prevails.
(6) STATES CAN BE REORGANISED by simple Parliament law (e.g. Telangana split from AP in 2014).
(7) GOVERNORS are appointed by the President (the Union), not elected by the state.
These features together make India a 'quasi-federal' or 'federation with a unitary bias' — designed for a country with great diversity and the need for strong national integration.

questions.question: What is the significance of fraternity in the Indian Constitution?
questions.answer: FRATERNITY in the Preamble means the spirit of BROTHERHOOD AND SOLIDARITY among all Indians. It is meant to (1) ensure the dignity of the individual — no one is to be looked down upon because of caste, religion, sex or language; (2) maintain the unity and integrity of the nation — Indians must see themselves as one people despite their diversity. In a country with the sheer scale of India's diversity — religious, linguistic, ethnic, regional, caste — fraternity is not automatic; it must be cultivated. Dr Ambedkar regarded fraternity as the most fundamental and most fragile of the three ideals: without it, justice and liberty would not stick. Constitutional protections against discrimination, secularism, single citizenship, and the duty 'to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood' (Article 51A(e)) are all rooted in this value.

questions.question: How is the Indian model of secularism different from the western (e.g. American or French) model?
Describe the salient features of the Indian political system.
questions.answer:
The Indian political system has six salient features:

1. WRITTEN CONSTITUTION: India has a long, detailed written Constitution (originally 395 articles) that is the supreme law of the land. All other laws and government actions must conform to it.

2. PARLIAMENTARY DEMOCRACY: India follows the British (Westminster) model. The President is the constitutional head of state; the Prime Minister, who leads the majority party in the Lok Sabha, is the head of government. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

3. FEDERAL STRUCTURE: Power is divided between the Union and the States via the Seventh Schedule's three lists (Union, State, Concurrent). India is 'quasi-federal' — has strong unitary features alongside federal ones.

4. UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE: Every Indian citizen aged 18+ has the right to vote, regardless of caste, religion, sex, education or property. India is the world's largest democracy by electorate.

5. INDEPENDENT JUDICIARY: The Supreme Court, High Courts and lower courts function independently of the executive. Judges have security of tenure. Courts have the power of JUDICIAL REVIEW — to strike down laws and actions that violate the Constitution.

6. RULE OF LAW + FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS: All persons are equal before the law. Citizens enjoy a set of constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights (Part III) that they can enforce in court.
